2-5.title: Do Things Together!
2-5.description: Learn how to remember to do good things!
2-5.script: Hi friend! Let's learn about doing things together!

explanations.habit: Something you do again and again
explanations.remember: Thinking about something you need to do

teachingMoments.content: Show simple actions like brushing teeth, then washing hands right after
Act out putting on shoes, then walking to door together

en.welcome: Hi friend! Do you brush your teeth? Yes! Do you wash your hands? Yes! Today we learn how to do things together!
en.mainContent: When you do one thing, you can do another thing too! Like this: After you brush teeth, you wash hands! After you put on shoes, you go to the door! After you wake up, you give a hug! See? One thing helps you remember the next thing! It's like making a chain. Brush teeth - wash hands. Get dressed - make bed. Eat breakfast - say thank you! When things go together, you don't forget! It's fun! Try it! Pick two things you do. Put them together. Now they're friends! They help each other!
keyPoints: Do one thing, then do another thing
Putting things together helps you remember
Make a chain of good things to do
Practice makes it easier
interactionPrompts: Can you brush your teeth?
What do you do after you wake up?
Let's put on shoes together!
Show me how you wash your hands!
en.wisdomMoment: When we put good things together, they become friends!
en.title: Building Better Habits - The Power of Habit Stacking

en.welcome: Hey! Have you ever forgotten to do something important? Like homework or feeding a pet? Today I'm going to teach you a super cool trick called habit stacking!
en.mainContent: Habit stacking is like building with blocks - you stack new habits on top of ones you already do! Here's how it works: Your brain loves patterns. You already do lots of things every single day without thinking - like brushing your teeth or eating breakfast. These are called automatic habits. Now here's the cool part: you can attach NEW habits to these automatic ones! It's like creating a recipe: After I [something you already do], I will [new thing you want to do]. For example: After I brush my teeth, I will read one page of a book. After I eat lunch, I will write in my journal. After I get home from school, I will put my backpack in its spot. The first action becomes a trigger - like a reminder alarm - for the second action! Scientists found that when you link habits this way, your brain connects them together. Soon, the new habit feels as automatic as the old one! You don't have to force yourself to remember anymore.
keyPoints: Habits are actions you do automatically without thinking hard
Habit stacking means attaching new habits to old ones
Use the formula: After I [old habit], I will [new habit]
The old habit becomes a trigger that reminds you
Your brain creates connections that make both habits automatic
interactionPrompts: What's something you do every single day without thinking?
Can you think of a new habit you'd like to build?
What could you stack that new habit onto?
Try creating your own habit stack using the formula!
en.wisdomMoment: Small habits stacked together can create big changes over time. You're building the person you want to become!
en.title: Building Better Habits - The Power of Habit Stacking

teachingMoments.content: Ask: What habits do you already have that happen automatically?
Create a sample habit stack: After I make my bed, I will do 5 jumping jacks

6-12.title: Building Better Habits - Habit Stacking
6-12.description: Discover how to build new habits using habit stacking!
6-12.script: Hey! Have you ever forgotten to do something important? Like homework or feeding a pet? Today I'm going to teach you a super cool trick called habit stacking!

en.welcome: What's up? So you want to build better habits but you keep forgetting or losing motivation, right? Same. But I learned this technique called habit stacking that actually works - and it's backed by neuroscience.
en.mainContent: Habit stacking is based on how your brain's neural pathways work. Every habit you have - checking your phone when you wake up, grabbing a snack after school - is a neural pathway that's been strengthened through repetition. Your brain has literally wired itself to make these actions automatic, which saves mental energy. Here's the strategy: instead of trying to build new habits from scratch using willpower alone, you piggyback them onto existing automatic behaviors. The formula is: After/Before I [current habit], I will [new habit]. For example: After I charge my phone at night, I will set out my workout clothes. Before I scroll social media, I will drink a glass of water. After I sit down for class, I will write the date in my notes. The key is specificity and realistic sizing. Don't stack 'I will work out for an hour' onto 'After I wake up.' Start with 'I will do 10 push-ups' or even 'I will put on workout shoes.' The goal is to create a trigger-action pattern that's so easy your brain can't resist. Once the pathway is established - usually takes about 2 months of consistency - you can expand it. What makes this different from random motivation is that you're working WITH your brain's existing wiring, not against it. You're essentially hacking your own neurology.
keyPoints: Habits are neural pathways strengthened through repetition
Habit stacking uses existing automatic behaviors as triggers
Formula: After/Before I [current habit], I will [new habit]
Start small and specific - build the pathway first, expand later
Consistency over 2 months creates automatic behavior
You're working with your brain's wiring, not fighting it
interactionPrompts: What's a habit you wish you had but keep failing to build?
What's something you do every single day without thinking?
How could you connect those two using the formula?
What's the smallest version of that new habit you could start with?
en.wisdomMoment: You don't need more discipline - you need better systems. Willpower is a muscle that gets tired. Habit stacks are structures that work even when you're exhausted.
en.title: Building Better Habits - The Power of Habit Stacking

teachingMoments.content: Discuss how willpower alone isn't sustainable - systems and structures work better
Analyze: Why do New Year's resolutions fail? (They lack triggers and systems)

13-17.title: Habit Stacking - Build Better Behaviors
13-17.description: Learn the neuroscience behind habit stacking
13-17.script: What's up? So you want to build better habits but you keep forgetting or losing motivation, right? Same. But I learned this technique called habit stacking that actually works - and it's backed by neuroscience.
objectives: Understand neural pathways and habit formation

en.welcome: Today we're exploring habit stacking - a behavioral design technique that leverages your brain's existing neural architecture to build sustainable personal systems. If you've struggled with habit formation, this is a game-changer.
en.mainContent: Habit stacking, popularized by James Clear and rooted in BJ Fogg's Behavior Model, works because it exploits the brain's pattern-recognition systems and the basal ganglia's role in automaticity. Every established habit represents a neural pathway that fires with minimal conscious effort. When you stack a new behavior onto an existing one, you're essentially creating a cue-routine-reward loop that requires less activation energy than building from scratch. The implementation formula is precise: After/Before I [established behavior], I will [new behavior]. The established behavior serves as both temporal anchor and cognitive trigger. For example: After I pour my morning coffee, I will write three items in my gratitude journal. Before I check email, I will review my top three priorities for the day. After I close my laptop at end of day, I will do 2 minutes of stretching. What makes this effective is specificity of trigger and realistic scaling. Research shows that habit formation follows a J-curve - initial effort is high, then it drops as automaticity develops, typically plateauing around 66 days. Common failure points include: vague triggers, oversized initial behaviors, and trying to stack too many new habits simultaneously. Best practice is to start with one clear stack, maintain it until it feels automatic, then add another. This compounds over time. Consider that 5 small habit stacks, each taking 2-3 minutes, adds up to a transformed daily routine of 10-15 productive minutes - which compounds to 60+ hours annually. You're not just building habits; you're architecting your default behavior patterns.
keyPoints: Habit stacking leverages existing neural pathways to reduce activation energy
Formula requires precise triggers: After/Before I [established], I will [new]
Automaticity develops around 66 days on average (J-curve pattern)
Common failures: vague triggers, oversized behaviors, stacking too many at once
Start with one stack, solidify it, then add more for compound effects
Small daily stacks create significant annual time investments through compounding
interactionPrompts: What established routines do you have that could serve as reliable triggers?
Which professional or personal behaviors would benefit your long-term goals?
What's the absolute smallest version of that behavior you could start with?
How would you track and measure your habit stack consistency?
en.wisdomMoment: Behavior change isn't about willpower - it's about architecture. You're not trying to be more disciplined; you're designing systems that make good behaviors inevitable and bad behaviors difficult. Your daily routine is your life in miniature.
en.title: Building Better Habits - The Power of Habit Stacking

teachingMoments.content: Map out your current daily routine and identify 3-5 potential trigger points

18-35.title: Habit Stacking - Behavioral Design Systems
18-35.description: Master the science and practice of habit stacking
18-35.script: Today we're exploring habit stacking - a behavioral design technique that leverages your brain's existing neural architecture to build sustainable personal systems. If you've struggled with habit formation, this is a game-changer.
objectives: Understand the neuroscience of habit formation

en.welcome: After decades of trying to change behaviors - some successfully, many not - I've learned that sustainable transformation isn't about dramatic overhauls. It's about intelligent stacking of small, consistent actions. Let me share what works.
en.mainContent: Habit stacking is elegantly simple in theory, humbling in practice, and transformative when done right. I've watched trends come and go - productivity hacks, life optimization systems, various self-help methodologies. What endures is this: behavioral change succeeds when it integrates seamlessly into the life you already live, not the idealized life you imagine. The power of habit stacking lies in its realism. After years of experimentation, I've learned that the formula - After I [established behavior], I will [new behavior] - works precisely because it doesn't ask you to become someone different. It works with who you already are. My morning routine evolved this way over 15 years: After I start the coffee maker, I do a 2-minute mobility exercise. After I pour my coffee, I review my calendar and identify my top priority. After I finish breakfast, I write three gratitude items. None of these required willpower after the first 2-3 months. They became me. Here's what I wish I'd known earlier: habit stacking is most powerful at life transitions. When I changed careers at 40, I built new professional habits onto existing personal ones. When my kids left for college, I reclaimed time by stacking reading and learning into the routines I'd already established. The transitions - whether chosen or forced by life - offer opportunities to rebuild your defaults. At this life stage, I see habit stacking not as productivity optimization but as legacy building. The person you are is the sum of what you do daily. By intentionally stacking behaviors aligned with your values, you're literally constructing your future self. The question isn't whether you have time. You have the same hours as everyone. The question is whether you're using your existing routines as foundations or letting them pass without building anything on them.
keyPoints: Sustainable change integrates into your actual life, not an idealized version
Habit stacking works because it accepts who you already are
Long-term success comes from behaviors that become automatic (2-3 months)
Life transitions offer powerful opportunities to rebuild routines
At midlife, habit stacking becomes legacy building - constructing your future self
The question isn't finding time, but using existing routines as foundations
interactionPrompts: Looking back, which habits have shaped who you've become?
What routines have survived your life transitions?
What values do you want your daily behaviors to reflect?
If you built 3 new habit stacks this year, what would they be?
en.wisdomMoment: You don't find time for what matters. You create systems where what matters happens automatically. Your habits are your autobiography - they tell the truth about your priorities. At this stage of life, the gift isn't more time; it's the wisdom to architect it well.
en.title: Building Better Habits - The Power of Habit Stacking

teachingMoments.content: Reflect on which habits from your 20s/30s still serve you today
Consider what legacy habits you want to pass to the next generation

36-60.title: Habit Stacking - Building Your Life Architecture
36-60.description: Wisdom on building sustainable habits over a lifetime
36-60.script: After decades of trying to change behaviors - some successfully, many not - I've learned that sustainable transformation isn't about dramatic overhauls. It's about intelligent stacking of small, consistent actions. Let me share what works.
objectives: Understand habit stacking through life experience
Learn to use transitions as habit-building opportunities

en.welcome: In eight decades, I've learned that we don't decide our lives in grand moments - we decide them in the small, repeated actions of ordinary days. Today I want to share the profound simplicity of habit stacking.
en.mainContent: When you've lived as long as I have, you see that humans are creatures of ritual. We crave routine. The Latin root of 'habit' is 'habere' - to have, to hold. Our habits are what we hold onto through life's changes - through wars, loves, losses, joys. I've seen the world transform dramatically, yet the fundamental truth remains: we become what we repeatedly do. Habit stacking is ancient wisdom wearing modern language. My grandmother didn't call it that, but she did it. After morning prayers, she tended her garden. After the family meal, she wrote in her journal. After sunset, she read to us. These stacks weren't productivity techniques - they were how she built a life of meaning. I've learned to stack habits at each stage of aging. In my 40s, after climbing stairs, I would pause to appreciate my working body. In my 60s, after my morning medication, I would write one memory to preserve. In my 80s, after my daily call with family, I sit quietly with gratitude. These stacks have given structure to a very long life. Here's what I want young people to understand: habits are the only possessions you take through every transition. Jobs end, children leave, bodies age, but habits - if built well - provide continuity. They are the through-line of identity. And here's what I want my peers to know: it's never too late to build new stacks. At 75, I stacked learning a new word onto my morning tea. At 80, I stacked a brief meditation onto taking my evening medication. Growth doesn't retire. The habit stacking formula - After I [do this], I will [do that] - is deceptively simple because profound truths often are. What you're really doing is building a life of intention, one small promise at a time. I've kept tens of thousands of small promises to myself over my lifetime. That's what character is - promises kept, especially the ones no one else witnesses.
keyPoints: Humans are creatures of ritual - we hold onto habits through life's changes
Habit stacking is ancient wisdom: linking meaningful actions creates purposeful living
Habits are the only possessions you carry through every life transition
Well-built habits provide continuity and identity across a lifetime
It's never too late to build new stacks - growth doesn't retire
Character is the sum of small promises kept to yourself over decades
The formula is simple because profound truths often are
interactionPrompts: What habits have you maintained throughout your entire adult life?
Which daily rituals give your life meaning and structure?
What wisdom would you stack into your remaining days?
If you could teach one habit to future generations, what would it be?
en.wisdomMoment: Life is long if you live it well. You live it well not through grand achievements but through small, good actions repeated faithfully. Habit stacking is the art of stringing pearls - each small action is a pearl, the formula is the string, and over years you create something beautiful. Your life is the necklace you've been making all along, one day at a time.
en.title: Building Better Habits - The Power of Habit Stacking

teachingMoments.content: Share a habit you've maintained for 40+ years and why it matters
